title: The Corridor
text:
<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> set down the second bowl without being asked.

"You're eating fast," she said.

"I have a job at midnight."

She looked at him. She had spent seventy years looking at men who had jobs at midnight, and it took her about half a second. Then she added a fish ball to the broth and said nothing. The wok rang its flat note, twice. <entity repo="motif" guid="019d6143-a8e2-727a-be75-32648e8aaa47">Rain</entity> worked the awning. Down the counter, a young woman in a <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> maintenance coverall was quietly telling her ramen that this was not the evening she'd planned.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> ate the fish ball. He paid exact and was in the alley by 21:45, <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> and <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> over his shoulder, the wet street smelling of ozone and freight oil.

His terminal was on the work channel. The posting was clean.

CONTRACT: ESCORT — ONE PERSON, ONE TRANSIT POINT.
SCOPE: SAFEHOUSE (ASHGRAVE FRINGE) TO DOCK 14-C (FERRYSIDE), BY 03:40.
CLIENT OF RECORD: [VERIFIED — SABLE COUNTER-INTELLIGENCE VETTED]
FEE: DOUBLE RATE PAST MIDNIGHT.
NOTES: CLIENT TRAVELS LIGHT. ROUTE AT DISCRETION.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT HAS REVIEWED PRIOR TRANSIT LOGS FOR THIS ROUTE. THREE INCIDENTS IN SEVEN MONTHS. NONE REPORTED. CLIENT NOTES THE DELTA.

He'd called Sable at twenty hundred. Sable was his fixer, contract broker, and primary employer—the rule, not the exception. The response came in text, no voice—her tell that she was somewhere that required quiet.

"Paper's clean," she'd said. "Client ran a counting house. Nine years. She gave two weeks' notice on a Tuesday, worked her <entity repo="contract" guid="d3a6c0e8-f2b1-7495-27e3-c8a0f6d2b145">last shift</entity> the Tuesday before last, and she's been in a transit safehouse since Wednesday." A pause, with the click of aperture rings in it. "The company she kept books for isn't named on the contract, <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafb-7b6b-bcbc-b8614f9d228f">samurai</entity>. I asked who she used to work for and the router gave me a shell."

"Shells?"

"One shell. Which means whoever's watching her thinks one shell is enough. The rate says they're wrong." Another click. "It's a clean contract. I'm not saying it's a quiet job."

"Standard terms," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"Yours or mine?"

"Both."

The line closed. He spent twenty minutes on the route, because the route was the whole job. He walked it in his head the way he'd walked its perimeter twice on foot—once for a failed contract, once just to see what the city looked like from that angle: every checkpoint, every place where an automated gate would count you and slow you and remember the count, every angle where a thing could come apart between two verifications. Then he'd eaten two bowls and let <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> add the fish ball.

He took the long way to the corridor entrance. The long way told him nothing, and that was its own kind of answer.

The fringe was quiet — the quiet that comes to fringe blocks when the people who know things have decided to be somewhere else. A lumen mouse sat on the conduit rail at the Langley corner and did not run when they passed. Its glow traced a pale crescent on the wet pipe. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> marked it and kept it in the corner of his sensors, open, in case it mattered.

At 00:17 they reached the corridor's east entrance.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stopped. Ms. Tanaka stopped beside him. The corridor ahead was dark, and it wasn't a power failure. The work lights in this run cycled on a timer — dusk to dawn, every fourth bank at half brightness to save power, the rest black. Standard fringe economy. Someone had turned two screws and killed the lot on purpose, to choose the conditions.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had walked this corridor two days ago, at noon. He'd learned the freight rail's maintenance hooks, the conduit boxes, the junction coupling twenty feet in that rang like a hammer-strike when you kicked it. He'd counted thirty-five feet to the first door frame — a maintenance alcove, eight inches deep, just enough to funnel whoever stood in its mouth into a tighter spot. He'd measured the low gap between the freight track and the floor. He'd counted the anchor bolts on the east wall: five of them, three feet apart, each one a handhold.

"Stay a step behind my left shoulder," he said, and walked in.

The corridor smelled of machine oil and old rain. Three feet past the mouth the air went cooler, and under the oil there was ozone — the sharp mineral bite of a space that had been sitting empty and charged, waiting.

He got sixty feet before the dark started moving.

The dark came at him in layers.

First the sound—boots on the freight rail, synchronized, which meant training. Three pairs, maybe four. The spacing was wrong for a standard ambush line; they were staggered vertically, using the conduit boxes for elevation. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s neuretics mapped it without asking: ground level, waist height, shoulder height. They'd done this before.

Ms. Tanaka's breathing had gone thin.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> moved her into the maintenance alcove—eight inches deep, exactly as he'd measured—and positioned himself in the mouth of it. The corridor's geometry was his now. It was also theirs. The question was which one of them understood it better.

"Don't move," he said. "Don't make sound."

The first two came from the east entrance behind them, cutting off retreat. The sound of their boots told him everything: heavy, deliberate, meant to be heard. Psychological weight. They expected him to run forward into the narrower trap.

He didn't move.

The ones ahead came next—three of them, spreading across the corridor width. The lead one had something in his hands. Not a gun. Something that made a small electrical hum when it powered up. A taser. Expensive. Mil-spec. The kind that worked through most body armor if you got close enough.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Corbin</entity>," the lead one called. His voice was flat, professional. "Step out of the alcove. <entity repo="motif" guid="019d6143-a8e1-7cd1-ab7c-1a4110a2ec8c">Hands</entity> visible. We're not here for the woman."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s hand was already on <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity>'s grip.

"They're not here for you," he said quietly to Ms. Tanaka. "That's what frightens me."

He stepped out of the alcove with both hands empty, moving slow, keeping his shoulders loose. The lead one—mid-forties, augmented across the left side of his face, military bearing—relaxed slightly. That was the tell. They'd been briefed to expect compliance.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> let them think they'd won that much.

The one with the taser moved in first, closing the distance to strike range. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was still six feet away. The corridor was wide enough for two to flank, which meant the third one was already angling for his left side, coming around the conduit box.

*Three seconds to contact.*

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s neuretics weren't predicting. They were reading. The lead one's weight was shifting. The flanker on the left was committed to the approach. The one with the taser had already decided the entry angle.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> moved backward—one step, clean, creating distance. The taser operator overcommitted, reaching for space that wasn't there anymore. His follow-through took him past <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s centerline.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s left arm came up and drove backward, two-handed, into the taser operator's throat.

Not a strike. A lever. The man's own momentum did the work. He went down hard, gasping, the taser skittering across the freight rail and into the dark.

The flanker on the left was already swinging—a baton, telescoping, mean. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> pivoted and caught it on his forearm. Pain lit up his wrists. His neuretics screamed. He pushed through it and pivoted again, using the baton's momentum to drive the flanker into the conduit box behind him.

The first man from the east came in with a short blade and the low crouch of someone good had trained. There were seven feet of corridor behind him, his people stacked single file, the next man six steps back and waiting his turn. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read the crouch and the low ceiling, stepped inside the man's commitment, and opened a long cut down the outside of his forearm, wrist to elbow — the cut you make when you need a hand to stop. The hand stopped. The blade rang off the freight rail somewhere east. The man stumbled back into the chest of the one behind him, and the two of them spent two seconds untangling. Two seconds was enough.

The second man tried to come around the first instead of through him. It was the smart read. But the narrow lane pushed him into the mouth of the maintenance alcove, and the alcove did what <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had counted on it to do — it caught the man's left shoulder on the door frame at the wrong moment, half a step before his weight was set. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> closed the gap, steered the stumble, and the man's own mass threw him sideways into the conduit boxes. The impact was hard.

Two conduit anchors sat at chest height on the east wall. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> already had a hand on the third when the third and fourth men came through.

They'd adjusted: one high, one low, taking everything the space would give them. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> caught the low man's weapon wrist at the seam where an aftermarket brace stood proud of the joint — the kind of hardware you bought when the joint had already gone once and you couldn't afford it going again — and the hand gave up the knife and the brace together. His weight was already going onto the conduit anchor. He pulled his feet off the floor for the half-second it took the high blade to pass beneath them, then came down on the high man's leading knee. Something that was not the floor took the weight. The high man went down and stayed down.

Four men east of center. Three more behind them, sorting themselves out.

He was counting, and the counting was the only thing left of him that felt like his own. Everything else — the wrist locks, the geometry, the twenty minutes he'd spent walking this corridor at noon — that was product, built by other hands, running on schedule. The count was his. He kept it because if he stopped keeping it, he wasn't sure what was left standing there instead of him.

Behind him, west, boots on wet composite. He didn't turn. He didn't have to — the junction box at his back would tell him the moment weight came off it.

"Six," Ms. Tanaka said, small, pressed into the corner where he'd put her. Not a question. A count of her own, offered because she had nothing else to give him.

He didn't answer. He put his shoulder into the fifth man and felt his rib file a complaint he had no room to hear. <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> stayed clean between them, because he'd learned a long time ago to use <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> so that it stayed clean — the flat, the spine, the pommel, everything but the edge that would have made the corridor a different kind of scene.

The corridor rang once — the junction coupling, twenty feet west, struck hard by something moving too fast in the dark. Not footsteps. Something bigger, coming down the same six feet of lane the fourteen had already spent, and coming into it from the wrong direction to be one of theirs.

The thing that rang the junction coupling was not a seventh man from the west.

It came into the light-spill of <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s own peripheral read — a shape moving low and wrong-fast, four points of contact, chassis sound instead of breath — and hit the sixth man from behind before <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had finished placing his weight. The sixth man went down without a sound. Whatever hit him didn't stop moving.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't have a name for it yet. He had geometry: it was coming east, down the center, at a speed that made the fourteen humans in the corridor look like they were standing still.

He put himself between it and Ms. Tanaka's corner without deciding to.

It resolved out of the dark six feet from him — quadruped, service-chassis gray, the kind of frame that used to walk a rail line checking bolt torque and had been doing something else for a long time now. Panels stripped to bare struts on one flank. No markings, no operator, no eyes — a sensor cluster where eyes would go, tracking him, tracking her, weighing which one cost less to remove first. An <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aabb-75d1-9889-22df001c8982">Iowan Behemoth</entity>, industrial stock, the sort built to move cargo through spaces where human hands weren't precise enough. The kind that didn't come with a kill switch because it had a priority list instead and the processing to work down it.

It came for him first. That told him something. He filed it and didn't have time to read it twice.

He took the hit on the flat of <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> instead of the edge, turning <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> to spare the metal and his own wrist, and the impact still drove him back a full step into the man he'd already put down at the conduit box. His feet found nothing solid. He went down on one knee, and the knee that took the floor was the one over the rib that had already filed its complaint. The complaint stopped being a complaint. It became a fact, bright and total, that sat behind his sternum and did not move when he told it to. The air left him in a shape that wasn't breath.

He came up anyway. He landed on his feet because his body remembered how to do that even when his lungs had forgotten. Coming up wasn't a choice. It was the only direction the body still knew.

The thing reset for another pass, tighter this time, more efficient — it had learned his guard in one exchange, the way good hardware does. It reared, all four legs off the ground for a fraction of a second, and dropped again into the line of sight, following the vector of his movement, the path a machine calculates as optimal. And <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> understood, with the flat clean certainty of a man reading his own gauge, that the next one would not be a rib. The next one would be worse, and there was no clever geometry in this corridor that made that not true. Fourteen men. One machine that moved like nothing human. Ms. Tanaka in the corner with six feet of packed dark between her and either.

*Every trick you have was built by someone else's hands. This is the one that's yours: you're <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafa-70f3-b5f5-be3330461876">still standing</entity>.*

He set his feet on the wet composite, found the count again — four down east, one down west, one thing that didn't count as a man at all — and went to meet it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood in the machine-oil dark. He didn't tally them. The corridor hadn't given him the room to, and it didn't matter now. He'd won — fourteen people down against the walls and the floor, the dock still in reach, Ms. Tanaka still pressed to the junction boxes. The win had a price, and the price was on his body. The forearm bled through the field strip he'd cinched tight with his teeth in a half-second between the fifth man and the sixth. The rib had a hard opinion about breathing that he wouldn't be able to ignore for long. His neuretics offered him a damage readout. He left it unread — not because he didn't want to know, but because knowing the exact numbers would only slow him down.

"Ms. Tanaka."

"I'm here," she said, from the junction boxes. Her voice had steadied, the way a voice does when the worst thing has passed and the next one hasn't come yet.

"We're moving. Same position. Stay close."

She came off the wall. In the dark she found his right shoulder by feel and fell into step behind it, easy about it. Nine years at someone's counting desk, he thought, teaches you how to stay near the person <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafa-70f3-b5f5-be3330461876">still standing</entity>.

He got her out the west end at 01:03.

The dock was a Ferryside loading pier: lake water and compressed fuel, and under the eastern breakwater the low hum of the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity>, its 19Hz signature buzzing in his back teeth and in the wet wood of the bollards. Dock 14-C was a third-tier berth — a mid-range cargo carrier on a mixed freight run. The purser at the gate was a small man with a clipboard who had worked enough 03:00 shifts to have opinions about paperwork and none about reasons.

Ms. Tanaka stopped at the dock gate.

She turned and looked at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s forearm, where the field strip had soaked dark at the edges, and then at his face.

"The contract," she said. "Whatever they paid you—"

"Was fine," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Walk in."

She hesitated. She was the kind of person who kept someone's books for nine years and then decided, one Tuesday, that she was done. A decision like that carries a weight that isn't only fear.

"I should have left three years ago," she said.

"Probably," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Walk in anyway."

She looked at the saya, and at the field strip, and at his face one more time. Then she walked in. The purser checked her boarding chit, noted the time — 03:34 — and closed the gate.

The ship ran its pre-cast sequence at 03:40 exactly. The thrusters came online low and old — combustion-based, the kind of drive that only survived on the maritime tier because nobody had ever bothered to upgrade the dock infrastructure to make it worth replacing. It traveled up through the bollard he was leaning on and into the rib, which had opinions about vibration. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> watched the running lights pull off the dock face, the carrier swinging its bow south toward the open lake, the flour on Ms. Tanaka's sleeves gone into the dark of the transit berths below with her.

He stood at the rail two minutes. Long enough to be sure. The beacon <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had wired under his battery tray had already pinged at 01:11 — she'd know where the bike was, and she'd work out the rest. He called for a medic pickup on the work channel — forearm laceration, possible rib fracture, non-critical — and got a forty-minute window and an instruction to stay visible. He sat down on a bollard to wait. The field strip had started weeping fresh at the edge again. He didn't cinch it. Bleeding that slow meant the wound was still trying to close on its own, and cinching it down only slowed the work. He'd learned that from someone. He couldn't remember who.

His terminal chirped.

STANDING CONTRACT — ADDENDUM.
CLIENT NOTES THE CONTRACT WAS MISPRICED BY THE MARKET.
CLIENT HAS ADJUSTED YOUR HAZARD SCHEDULE. RETROACTIVELY.

He read it twice. He put the terminal away.

The medic came at 04:15 — a quiet woman named Rue, with a field kit and the easy economy of someone who worked the dock district's early hours and had long since stopped asking about corridors. She cleaned the forearm and re-stripped it, cutting the field strip away with scissors that moved like they already knew where the bleeding would be. The cut ran two inches along the inside, deep but clean, a clean furrow from something with an edge, already clotting at the rim.

"This one's fine," she said, and reached for the closure. Not stitches — those scarred thick — but the polymer kit that ran thread through the dermis and left no mark, the kind that cost more and mattered to a man who couldn't afford to be recognized by his wounds. She worked it with the focus of someone who had done it ten thousand times and still treated it like it counted. "The rib's the problem."

"Cracked," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"Cracked or broken, doesn't matter to me. Matters to you in about six hours when you try to sleep on it." She pressed on the exhale, reading the damage through touch. Hairline. She confirmed it, taped it firm — the elastic going round in a pattern that limited rotation without stopping breath — and handed him a small packet of painkillers he wouldn't take before a job and could take now.

"You'll favor the arm," she said.

"I know," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"Two weeks minimum. More if you don't favor it. And you'll want to favor it, which means you'll move wrong and make it worse."

"I know that too."

She packed her kit. He paid her rate plus the dock-hour premium, exact. She left without asking what the corridor had looked like. Dock medics learn that early and keep it their whole careers.

The rib would be the louder bill. The forearm would stiffen by morning, which meant his draw would be slower for two weeks, which meant every job in that window was now a different job than the one he'd planned for. He sat on the bollard, breathing careful around the rib, and thought about Golan.

He'd passed Golan's block on the way to the dock — the parts dealer on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity> who'd sold him mesh-repair supplies for seven years. Golan kept a second-floor shop with a yellow security light over the door that <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> could read from a quarter mile off. He'd looked up out of habit on the approach, and the yellow light was off. Through the glass of the street-level lobby, Golan was standing at the inner door, watching him. When <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> tried the lobby handle — just the lobby, just the handle — Golan looked at him for three seconds and did not move.

One closed door. And it wouldn't stop at one.

Fourteen <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity> crew — salaried, professional — had been hurt badly in a dark choke over one counting-room clerk with flour on her sleeves. <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity> would collect for that, slowly, through every vendor and carrier and parts dealer who had a standing arrangement with them and would rather close a door than explain an exception. That was the arithmetic of <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a94e-7740-8aa9-4b82bbd9a223">the Gray Zone</entity>: they didn't come for the man first, they came for the people who kept him running, because the supply line was the softest place to press and the cheapest to hold. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had spent eleven years building those arrangements into something he leaned on. Now they'd lean back.

He sat on the bollard and waited to find out how much of him would be left in the morning.

The lake was grey, the dawn still an hour out. South of the breakwater, the carrier's running light shrank to a point, then to nothing. Then there was only the water and the hum of the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> underneath everything, that 19Hz signature that lived in the wet wood of the bollard and in his back teeth and in the space between one breath and the next.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat there a while longer.

Nine years at a counting desk. A decision like that isn't only fear — it's a woman who woke up one Tuesday and decided the numbers she'd been asked to keep clean were dirtier than she could carry anymore. He'd read a version of that decision on his own ledger more times than he'd admit to Rue or to anyone with a needle and thread. *You made yourself the corridor so she wouldn't have to be.* He didn't let the thought finish. He stood instead, favoring the rib, and the standing hurt more than the sitting had.

The <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">Continuity Office</entity> would have a file open on this by breakfast — some clerk logging a transit-berth boarding at 03:34, cross-referencing it against fourteen <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity> casualties two blocks inland, and deciding whether the correlation was worth a flag. He didn't know that. He knew only that the yellow light over Golan's shop was off, and that the light being off was its own kind of paperwork.

The gate at 14-C had already reset for the next boarding call. No one there remembered Ms. Tanaka's name, or needed to. That was the whole point of a <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aa8f-796a-8b70-7076ec482c7f">clean exit</entity> — the door closes, and the world downstream of the door doesn't know there was ever a woman standing in it with flour on her sleeves and a decision she'd finally made.

He didn't tally what it cost him. The rib did that arithmetic on its own, every time he breathed — two weeks of favoring it, which meant two weeks of every job being a different job than the one he'd planned for. The forearm would stiffen by morning. The draw would be slower. And the market would notice that too, the way the market noticed everything a man couldn't hide in the way he stood.

Golan's door stayed shut in his mind's eye a beat longer than it should have. He put it down — not solved, just set aside, the way you set aside a blade you can't sharpen standing in the rain — and started walking back toward the bike, and toward whatever waited for him now that <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity> knew his name attached to their bruises.
